documents: Luo & Zhang 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL098864, published paper (PDF, 10 pages); Supporting Information S1 not supplied
pages_convention: printed journal pages (printed as 'n of 10'; identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: blowing snow impacts over this region have been vastly understudied

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how blowing snow affects the modeled surface energy budget and surface mass balance of Larsen C Ice Shelf over a full melt season. They frame it against spread among SMB model estimates and the short span of their earlier case study (L21).
steps.quote: herein, we examine blowing snow impacts on the SEB and SMB modeling over LCIS during the melt season of November–February, 2017–2018

steps.action: The authors take up WRF-ice, the model developed in their own earlier work. It couples thermodynamic sea ice, the two-moment Déry & Yau blowing-snow scheme, and one-dimensional snow-firn physics.
steps.quote: a snow-ice enhanced model referred to as WRF-ice has been developed to better represent the air-snow-ice interactions in the polar region

steps.action: The authors improve the snow-firn physics of WRF-ice with three changes: a water-weighted firn density profile, an irreducible liquid water content of 4% of pore volume, and the Pflug et al. (2019) percolation scheme.
steps.quote: further improvements to the snow-firn physics of WRF-ice have been made in this study

steps.action: The authors compare the modeled firn density profile (about 300 to 400 kg m-3 over the top 5 m) with published densification observations.
steps.quote: which is generally consistent with previous snow densification observations

steps.action: The authors design a paired experiment: a 4-month ERA5-forced WRF-ice run with nested 15 km and 3 km domains, made once with blowing snow on (CNTL) and once with it off (Blow-off).
steps.quote: A total of two simulations named control (CNTL) and Blow-off are conducted with the blowing snow processes activated in CNTL and deactivated in Blow-off

steps.action: The authors validate CNTL near-surface sea level pressure, 2-m temperature, humidity and 10-m wind against 10 surface stations. They attribute the mismatch at Cape Framnes to observational bias and the residual biases to surface type and terrain.
steps.quote: the time series of daily averaged sea level pressure (SLP) observed at all stations except Cape Framnes are well reproduced by CNTL

steps.action: The authors validate CNTL skin temperature against MODIS ice surface temperature on six days with more than 60% valid coverage. They attribute the roughly 10 K cold outliers to overpass time and cloud contamination.
steps.quote: Modeled skin temperature over LCIS is validated against the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) ice surface temperature (IST).

steps.action: The authors compute monthly CNTL SMB and its budget terms. Precipitation and runoff dominate, and SMB is negative only along the east coast in December and January.
steps.quote: contributions from precipitation and runoff dominate the LCIS SMB

steps.action: The authors compare the modeled runoff-to-meltwater ratio with the range in Gilbert and Kittel (2021). They also compare the runoff pattern with observed surface drainage on Antarctic ice shelves.
steps.quote: The ratio of runoff and surface meltwater production herein is close to 20%, which is overall within that corresponding range

steps.action: The authors difference CNTL minus Blow-off for the SMB and SEB components. They find the largest blowing-snow transport (Enet) signal in November under northwesterly downslope flow, and blowing-snow sublimation of about 3 to 4 mm in November and December.
steps.quote: Differences of SMB (Equation 1, Figure 4a) and SEB (Equation 2, Figure 4b) components between the CNTL and Blow-off simulations

steps.action: The authors compare the magnitude of modeled blowing-snow sublimation with the ERA15-based estimate of Déry and Yau (2002).
steps.quote: These values are generally consistent with the magnitude of Sbs over Antarctica derived by Déry and Yau (2002)

steps.action: From the paired-run differences the authors trace a mechanism chain. Sublimation moistens and cools the air, which raises precipitable water, cloud and precipitation and reduces the latent heat flux, sensible heat flux and surface sublimation. Together with radiative changes this gives a positive SEB anomaly and more melt and runoff.
steps.quote: Moistening and cooling due to Sbs reduce vertical humidity and temperature gradient between surface and lower atmosphere

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that blowing snow produces positive SEB and negative SMB anomalies over most of LCIS. They put the 99th-percentile anomalies at about 10% to 20% of the monthly values.
steps.quote: blowing snow contributes to negative SMB and positive SEB anomalies over most LCIS

tree.answer: Blowing-snow effects on the SEB and SMB of Larsen C over a melt season, assumed real from earlier work
No; the blowing-snow contribution is not observed over LCIS and is isolated by model on/off runs
Evaluate the model, then quantify the blowing-snow impact on the SEB and SMB components
No stated rival hypotheses; only blowing snow on versus off
Conditions set in the model: blowing snow switched off in a paired run
Only model realism is checked, against stations, MODIS and published magnitudes; no sensitivity or ensemble tests of the blowing-snow effect
Kept: positive SEB and negative SMB anomaly from blowing snow

end.claim: In the WRF-ice simulation of the 2017–2018 melt season, blowing snow causes a positive surface energy budget anomaly and a net negative surface mass balance anomaly over Larsen C Ice Shelf. Blowing-snow sublimation and the extra melt and runoff outweigh enhanced precipitation, reduced surface sublimation and blowing-snow deposition.

decisive_move.sentence: The claim exists only through the CNTL minus Blow-off differencing of the paired simulations; there is no observation of the blowing-snow effect itself.

gates.evidence: The question about blowing snow directed the design of the paired on/off runs (p. 4), but no data acquisition was hypothesis-driven. The station and MODIS validation tests near-surface conditions and skin temperature (pp. 4-5), not the blowing-snow impact, so the headline difference could not fail an observational test. Nothing is stated as fixed in advance.

novelty_claims.quote: this study represents the first effort in modeling SMB and SEB over LCIS and examining the blowing snow impacts with a multi-moment blowing snow module

limits: No review file or Supporting Information was supplied, so Figures S1–S13 and Tables S1–S2 are cited only as the main text describes them. Composition is none_fits: the walk is model improvement, then validation of the control run, then a single counterfactual on/off experiment. There are no rivals, no observational test of the blowing-snow effect and no repetition across events or seasons, so none of trace_series, capability_first or strong_inference fits. Claim status estimate_with_resolution is generous: the anomalies are given at monthly and spatial resolution (99th percentiles, LCIS means), but no uncertainty is quantified. There is one run per configuration with no ensemble, so whether the differences exceed internal model variability is not shown (inference). There are no sensitivity tests of the new firn parameterizations or of blowing-snow parameters. Runoff is unvalidated, as the authors acknowledge (p. 5). Blowing snow itself (occurrence, transport, sublimation) is not validated against observations such as CALIPSO; the only check is consistency with Déry & Yau (2002). The study covers one season, and the authors call for longer studies (p. 8). On p. 6 the text labels SMB as Equation 1 and SEB as Equation 2, the reverse of p. 2. Sub-claim: the WRF-ice capability for near-surface conditions over the melt season is at status capability_characterized (pp. 4-5, 8).

disagreements.target: Luo et al. (2021) (L21), the authors' own case study
disagreements.support: The authors extend a few-day case study to a full 4-month melt season over LCIS.
disagreements.quote: However, study in L21 spans only a few days, thus necessitating long-term studies

disagreements.target: Lenaerts and van den Broeke (2012), RACMO2 with a one-moment blowing snow scheme
disagreements.support: The authors cite studies showing that multi-moment schemes give more realistic particle size distributions and transport and sublimation rates, and they use a two-moment scheme.
disagreements.quote: Studies have noted that multi-moment blowing snow scheme can yield more realistic blowing snow particle size distributions, transport rate, and sublimation rate

disagreements.target: Firn density profile from Schytt (1958) used by Yao et al. (2016)
disagreements.support: Because firn densifies faster in the wet-snow zone, the authors replace the profile with a water-weighted profile based on Dome C.
disagreements.quote: the firn density profile from Schytt (1958) used by Yao et al. (2016) is updated to

disagreements.target: Cape Framnes station sea level pressure observations
disagreements.support: Observed SLP at Cape Framnes is about 8 hPa below both the model and nearby Robertson Island, which the authors read as an observational bias.
disagreements.quote: suggesting a significant observational bias might exist at Cape Framnes

disagreements.support: Cold IST outliers of about 10 K are not seen at the stations, and the authors attribute them to overpass time and cloud contamination.
disagreements.quote: suggesting quite different overpass time might be used in the IST data sets

alternatives_considered.chosen: Water-weighted firn density profile (Dome C dry-snow profile plus a meltwater term)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Firn density profile from Schytt (1958) used by Yao et al. (2016)
alternatives_considered.reason: Firn densifies more rapidly in the wet-snow zone because meltwater raises density

alternatives_considered.alternatives: One-moment scheme (Déry & Yau, 1999) as used in RACMO2 by Lenaerts and van den Broeke (2012)
alternatives_considered.reason: Multi-moment schemes yield more realistic particle size distributions and transport and sublimation rates
